name: Manager Leverage and Communication

positioning.oneLineSummary: Tests whether managers create leverage through clear ownership, unblocking, development, and communication rather than becoming permanent bottlenecks.
positioning.productLabel: Manager Leverage Lens — based on Claire Hughes Johnson's public Scaling People materials
notAClaimOf: one span of control fitting every team

attribution.display: Based on Claire Hughes Johnson's public Scaling People materials

neutralParaphrase: As a team grows, a manager still practices core management but shifts from solving every task toward clarifying outcomes, allocating ownership, coaching or unblocking at the right level, and communicating consistently across distance and layers.

locator.value: Transcript p. 1, 00:00-02:53: managing managers and leaders, unblocking, feedback, team unit, and intentional scaled communication
Q&A on management scoping work, matching people, developing individuals, goals, monitoring results, and leadership distinction
Lines 33-41: explorer rather than lecturer, observations, questions, and partnership
Transcript lines 198-204 and surrounding discussion: leader feedback, standards, and changing behavior so the team can grow

requiredConditions: The company has managers or leaders responsible for work through others.
Manager behavior can be reviewed through decisions and work outcomes.
The analysis respects employee privacy and context.

requiredEvidence.description: Manager outcomes, scope, team, decision rights, escalation path, and delegation boundaries.
Representative decisions showing who owned work, when the manager intervened, and whether intervention unblocked or displaced ownership.
One-to-one, team, goal, feedback, development, and scaled communication practices with content and audience.
Delivery, quality, decision speed, regretted attrition, internal mobility, role clarity, and team dependency on the manager.

decisionQuestions: Which decisions can the team make without the manager?
When does the manager coach, unblock, decide, or escalate?
Does intervention develop capability or create recurring dependence?
Can important context reach people beyond direct personal contact?
What happens to decisions and delivery when the manager is absent?
positiveSignals: Decision rights and escalation thresholds are understood.
Managers ask, observe, and unblock before taking over.
Teams deliver and decide during manager absence.
Communication is consistent, authentic, specific, and adapted to audience.
Manager involvement changes as reports become managers or leaders.
redFlags: Every consequential decision waits for one leader.
Delegation transfers tasks but not authority or context.
Managers answer before diagnosing the problem.
Scaled communication becomes generic performance theater.
High team output depends on hidden manager heroics.
disconfirmingEvidence: Centralized intervention is temporary during an incident, turnaround, or regulated decision.
A technically deep manager remains appropriately involved in a critical design decision.
Apparent dependency reflects a newly formed team with a time-bound capability plan.
A small team rationally shares most decisions.
contraindications: Do not prescribe one span of control or meeting format.
Do not treat manager absence as the only delegation test.
Do not infer management quality from popularity.
Do not use private employee communications without authorization.

instructions: Map role, decisions, ownership, escalation, and communication.
Trace representative interventions and their later effects.
Test whether capability and autonomy increase over time.
Review appropriate counterexamples for crisis, safety, or stage.
Conclude leverage-building, balanced, bottlenecked, absent, or insufficient.

sourceReliability.medium: Role maps and selected decision records.
sourceReliability.high: Repeated decisions, delivery outcomes, absence tests, and consent-based evidence converge.

evidenceStrength.high: Longitudinal evidence shows growing team capability and resilient delivery.

evidenceCoverage.high: Rights, interventions, communication, development, outcomes, absence, and counterevidence covered.

applicabilityConfidence.high: Execution materially depends on multiple managers or leaders.

judgmentConfidence.medium: Traceable examples support a bounded judgment.
judgmentConfidence.high: Longitudinal ownership and outcome evidence supports the conclusion.

empiricalQualifications: Centralization and decentralization can each be appropriate by stage and risk.
Team outcomes have many causes beyond management.

rights.notes: Public author materials are neutrally paraphrased.

openIssues: Define evidence thresholds for founder bottleneck versus rational early-stage centralization.
